stem: An adolescent has a persistent pattern of aggression toward people and animals, deliberate property destruction, and serious rule violations. Which condition is most consistent with these findings?

options.A: Oppositional defiant disorder characterized mainly by persistent argumentative, defiant, or vindictive behavior without this pattern of serious rights violations.
options.B: Attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder characterized primarily by developmentally inappropriate inattention and/or hyperactivity-impulsivity.
options.C: Conduct disorder characterized by an ongoing pattern that violates the basic rights of others or major societal norms and rules.
options.D: Typical adolescent behavior because persistent aggression, property destruction, and serious rule violations are expected developmental findings.

rationale: Conduct disorder involves an ongoing pattern in which the basic rights of others or major societal norms or rules are violated. Recognized behavior categories include aggression toward people or animals, destruction of property, deceitfulness or theft, and serious rule violations. The pattern in the stem therefore best fits conduct disorder, not typical adolescent behavior or a disorder defined primarily by defiance or inattention.
educational_objective: Recognize the core behavioral pattern of conduct disorder and distinguish it from oppositional defiant disorder, ADHD, and normal adolescent behavior.
source_organization: National Library of Medicine / NCBI Bookshelf
source_document_title: Nursing Health Promotion — Chapter 7 Mental Health Conditions, Section 7.15 Behavior Disorders
source_locator: Section 7.15, Conduct Disorder; Assessment of Conduct Disorder (Recognizing Cues): ongoing rights/norm violations with aggression, property destruction, deceit/theft, or serious rule violations
source_claim_supported: Conduct disorder is an ongoing pattern violating others' rights or societal norms/rules and includes aggression, property destruction, deceit/theft, and serious rule violations; these behaviors differ from ordinary age-typical defiance.
blueprint_source_organization: National Council of State Boards of Nursing (NCSBN)
blueprint_locator: Printed p.10, Psychosocial Integrity — mental health concepts and behavioral assessment
blueprint_topic: Psychosocial Integrity — behavior disorders / conduct disorder

source_original.stem: A nurse is assessing an adolescent client with a pattern of behavior that includes aggression toward people and animals, destruction of property, and serious violations of rules, though a teacher dismisses this as just typical rebellious teenage behavior. This presentation is most consistent with:

options.A: Typical adolescent rebellion without persistent violations of others' rights
options.B: A mood disorder defined mainly by sadness without serious behavioral violations
options.C: Conduct disorder with persistent aggression, destruction, or serious rule violations
options.D: A transient adjustment response without a persistent pattern of harmful behavior

source_original.rationale: Conduct disorder is characterized by a repetitive, persistent pattern of behavior in which the basic rights of others or major age-appropriate societal norms are violated, including aggression toward people or animals, destruction of property, deceitfulness or theft, and serious rule violations, distinguishing it from typical adolescent behavior variations.
source_original.source_detail: Persistent aggression/rights violations, property destruction, deceit/theft, and serious rule violations; accessed 2026-08-14.

correction_summary: Replaced the older generic StatPearls source with the 2025 NCBI nursing text, tightened the stem, made distractors clinically meaningful by contrasting ODD and ADHD, and reduced difficulty from hard to easy because the final item tests direct recognition of a classic behavioral pattern.

audit_findings.source_authority: NCBI Bookshelf nursing text (2025) with DSM-5-TR-based content; NCSBN 2026 Test Plan
audit_findings.currentness: The 2025 NCBI nursing chapter was current and accessible on 2026-08-17.
audit_findings.claim_audit: The stem's aggression, property destruction, and serious rule violations directly match the source's recognized conduct-disorder behavior categories.

distractor_audit.A: ODD emphasizes angry/irritable, argumentative/defiant or vindictive behavior and does not best explain the severe rights-violating pattern in the stem.
distractor_audit.B: ADHD's core pattern is inattention and/or hyperactivity-impulsivity, not the specified rights violations.
distractor_audit.D: The source explicitly distinguishes persistent or severe disruptive behavior from ordinary developmental defiance.

audit_findings.ambiguity_second_answer: The severe persistent rights/norm violations make C uniquely best; none of the alternatives accounts for the full pattern.
audit_findings.cueing: All options are plausible developmental/psychiatric categories; the answer requires pattern recognition.
audit_findings.blueprint: Recognition of maladaptive child/adolescent behavioral patterns maps to Psychosocial Integrity.
audit_findings.independent_second_pass: Rechecked NCBI 2025 Section 7.15 and compared the stem against the conduct-disorder, ODD, ADHD, and normal-development distinctions; C remained uniquely correct.
